passage:
Counsellor's note, haematology ward, Tuesday

Damini, twenty-five, came in for her second review with her father, Hemant. He answered every question the doctor asked her, and he had asked the ward staff to give test results to him first "so she won't be upset."

When he stepped out for tea, Damini said to me, voice tight, "I love him. But I feel like a child in my own illness."

I suggested she tell him two lists: what help she wants, and what she wants to decide herself. She practised it with me.

When he came back, she said, "Papa, I want you at every appointment. I want you to drive me. But I want to hear the results first, and I want to choose about the treatment timing. I can handle hard news. I'd rather share it with you than have you carry it alone."

He was quiet, then his eyes filled. "I just don't want you frightened."

"I'm already frightened, Papa. Be frightened with me."

I have updated the ward notes: results go to Damini first.

qa.q: What had Hemant asked the ward staff to do?
qa.a: Give test results to him first "so she won't be upset."

qa.q: What did Damini feel about her father's protectiveness?
qa.a: She felt loved but smothered, like a child in her own illness, and frustrated at being left out.

qa.q: What approach helped Damini talk to her father, and why?
qa.a: Listing what help she wanted and what she wanted to decide herself, which let her keep him close while taking back her own choices.

qa.q: How does Hemant see his own behaviour?
qa.a: Hemant sees it as protecting Damini from fear, which shows his love, until she asks him to share the fear with her.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a parent who manages everything and hides results out of fear, and a young woman who tells him what help she wants and what she will decide herself.

passage:
Gurleen's diary. Sunday night.

I found out today that Mummy and Papa knew about my scan result for three days before telling me. Manoj, my brother, let it slip. They'd told the doctor to "go slowly with her."

I was so angry I couldn't speak at dinner. I'm twenty-four, not four.

Later Mummy came into my room with haldi milk and sat on the bed, and I saw her hands were shaking. She said, "We were so scared, beta. We didn't know how to say it."

And I understood. The hiding was fear. The fear was love.

So I told her, calmly, what I want. I want them at appointments. I want Mummy's food and Papa's jokes. But I want to hear everything first, from the doctor, and I'll decide the big things myself. I promised I'd tell them the hard parts too.

She nodded and held my hand for a long time. Tomorrow I'll say the same to Papa.

qa.q: How long did the parents know the scan result before telling Gurleen?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What changed in Gurleen's feelings when Mummy's hands were shaking?
qa.a: Gurleen's anger softened into understanding, seeing that the hiding came from fear and love.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask for, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: Gurleen asked for company and help, but to hear everything first and decide the big things, and promised to share the hard parts, which respects both sides.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the decision to hide the result?
qa.a: Mummy saw it as protecting Gurleen, because they were scared and didn't know how to say it.

grounding: The diary shows a young adult whose parents hide news out of fear, understanding it as love, and telling them what help they want and what they will decide themselves.

passage:
Dear Zubin,

I've written this four times. Here's the plain version.

When I told you about the diagnosis in March, you hugged me hard and said, "Anything you need." Then you went quiet. No calls. You didn't come to the hospital. I heard from Aman you were at the match on the day of my surgery.

It hurt, more than I'll admit. At first I thought you'd stopped caring.

But I know you. You were the one who couldn't go to your grandfather's funeral because you didn't know what to do with your face. I think this is the same. You don't know what to say.

So I'll tell you. You don't have to say anything wise. Send me a stupid meme on Tuesdays. Come on Saturday and watch cricket with me, even if we just shout at the screen.

I miss you. That's all.

Lokesh

qa.q: What did Zubin say when Lokesh first shared the diagnosis?
qa.a: "Anything you need."

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel when Zubin went quiet?
qa.a: Lokesh felt hurt and at first feared Zubin had stopped caring.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that could bring Zubin back?
qa.a: Lokesh named the hurt gently and told Zubin exactly how to help, a meme on Tuesdays and a cricket visit on Saturday.

qa.q: Why might Zubin have disappeared?
qa.a: Zubin probably felt uncomfortable and helpless, not knowing what to say, as at the grandfather's funeral Zubin couldn't face.

grounding: The letter shows someone whose friend disappeared after a diagnosis out of discomfort, naming the hurt and telling the friend simple ways to help.

passage:
"You want to know who stayed? I'm Hemant, and honestly, the list surprised me.

When I got sick last year, three of my closest college friends vanished. Parveen, my best friend since school, didn't call for six weeks. I was hurt. I lay awake thinking, so that's what I meant to them.

Then Parveen's sister told me something. Parveen had been crying every time she picked up the phone, and then putting it down. She didn't know what to say.

So I called her. I said, 'You don't have to say anything right. Just come and eat samosas and tell me office gossip.'

She came the next day, with samosas and a lot of guilty tears. After that, every Thursday.

The other two I still hear from sometimes. That's okay. People are clumsy with illness. But I tell anyone who's sick now: tell your friends what you need. And hold on tight to the ones who show up."

qa.q: How long did Parveen go without calling?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Parveen didn't call?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and wondered at night what Hemant had really meant to those friends.

qa.q: What turned things around with Parveen?
qa.a: Hemant called Parveen and said exactly what would help: no perfect words, just samosas and office gossip.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling during those six weeks?
qa.a: Parveen felt upset and helpless, crying each time she picked up the phone because she didn't know what to say.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone whose friends disappear during illness out of discomfort, telling a friend how to help and cherishing those who stay.

passage:
I'm Pranav. When Minakshi told our group she had cancer, I didn't call her for a week. I was terrified of saying something stupid.

Then my mother said, "You're not scared for her. You're scared for yourself. Go."

So I went. I brought her favourite masala peanuts and sat on the end of her bed. I didn't say "It's all part of a plan" or "You're so strong." I'd read that people hate those. I just asked, "How are you, really?"

She talked for an hour. I mostly listened. I didn't try to fix anything.

Before leaving, I said, "I'm driving you to chemo on Wednesdays. Don't argue."

She laughed and didn't argue.

I still said wrong things sometimes. Once I cried more than she did. She said later that didn't matter. What mattered was that I kept coming.

qa.q: What did Pranav bring on the first visit?
qa.a: Minakshi's favourite masala peanuts.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling during the week he didn't call?
qa.a: Pranav felt terrified and anxious about saying something stupid to Minakshi.

qa.q: What did Pranav get right on the visit?
qa.a: Showing up, asking how she really was, listening instead of fixing, avoiding clichés, and offering specific help with Wednesday rides.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Pranav's visits?
qa.a: Minakshi values that Pranav kept coming more than any perfect words, even when Pranav said wrong things.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone afraid of saying the wrong thing to an ill friend, who shows up, listens more than fixes, avoids clichés and offers specific help.

passage:
Football coach's note, Sunday league, week 9

Mohit, our goalkeeper, missed three games. His teammates heard he's having treatment for a serious illness. Most of them have gone quiet in the group chat, not knowing what to say.

Amandeep has not. After training on Thursday I saw Amandeep standing by the gate, typing and deleting a message for ten minutes, clearly worried about getting it wrong. I asked what was wrong. "I don't want to say something stupid," Amandeep said.

I said the words matter less than showing up.

Today Amandeep told me what happened. Amandeep went to Mohit's flat, didn't say "stay positive," just listened to him talk about the treatment and the boredom. Then Amandeep offered two specific things: dal on Mondays and a lift to hospital on Fridays.

Mohit texted the group tonight for the first time in weeks: "Thanks, Amandeep. Rest of you, come too."

Next step: I've asked the team to take turns with Amandeep's lifts.

Coach

qa.q: What two things did Amandeep offer Mohit?
qa.a: Dal on Mondays and a lift to hospital on Fridays.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling while typing and deleting the message?
qa.a: Amandeep felt anxious and afraid of saying something stupid to Mohit.

qa.q: What did Amandeep get right with Mohit?
qa.a: Amandeep showed up, listened instead of saying "stay positive", and offered specific help like meals and lifts.

qa.q: How does Mohit seem to feel about Amandeep's visit?
qa.a: Mohit seems grateful and less alone, thanking Amandeep and inviting the others to come too.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young person afraid of saying the wrong thing to an ill friend, who shows up, listens, avoids clichés and offers specific help.

passage:
"You've been going to the church prayer group every evening since the diagnosis," Thomas said, handing his brother a cup of tea. "Is it helping?"

"More than anything," Mohit said. "When they pray for me, I stop shaking. I sleep."

"Good. Then keep going."

Mohit looked at the tea. "There's a man who came last week. A healer. He says if I have enough faith, I can stop the chemotherapy. He says the medicines show doubt."

Thomas set his own cup down. "What does Father Joseph say?"

"He says pray and take the medicine. God works through doctors too."

"And what do you think?"

Mohit was quiet a long time. "I think I'm scared of the chemo. And the healer's offer sounds easier."

"It sounds easier," Thomas said gently. "It isn't safer. Keep the prayers. Keep the chemo. Both."

Mohit nodded slowly. "Will you come to the hospital Thursday?"

"And to prayer group after," Thomas said.

qa.q: What does Father Joseph say about prayer and medicine?
qa.a: "Pray and take the medicine. God works through doctors too."

qa.q: Why did the healer's offer tempt Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit felt scared of the chemotherapy, so a promise to stop it through faith sounded easier.

qa.q: Which choice does Thomas encourage, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping both the prayers and the chemotherapy, because faith brings Mohit comfort while treatment is what's safe, and a miracle promise replacing it is dangerous.

qa.q: How does Thomas see the prayer group?
qa.a: Thomas is glad it helps Mohit sleep and stop shaking, and even offers to go with him.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man finding solace in prayer during illness while keeping medical treatment, and rejecting a healer's promise that would replace it.

passage:
I'm Ramesh. The year I was ill, the temple saved me in a way I can't fully explain.

Every morning before my dialysis, I went to the small Ganesha shrine near the hospital. The bells, the smell of camphor, the old priest who never asked questions but always gave me extra prasad. For twenty minutes I wasn't a patient. I was just someone praying.

My friend Sumit came with me most days. He's not religious, but he'd sit on the steps and wait.

Once, a man at the temple told me about a swami whose holy water had cured kidney disease. "Stop the machines," he said. "Have faith."

I told Sumit. He didn't mock me. He just asked, "What would your doctor say?"

I knew. I kept the dialysis and the shrine, both, for a whole year. Today I still go to that shrine, to say thank you. And I'm still here to do it.

qa.q: Who came with Ramesh to the shrine most days?
qa.a: Ramesh's friend Sumit.

qa.q: What did Ramesh feel during the twenty minutes at the shrine?
qa.a: Ramesh felt calm and comforted, no longer just a patient but someone praying.

qa.q: What choice did Ramesh make about the holy water, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Ramesh kept both the dialysis and the prayers, because faith brought comfort while treatment kept Ramesh alive.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Ramesh's faith?
qa.a: Sumit respects it without sharing it, waiting on the steps, but gently reminds Ramesh to think about the doctor's view.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone finding solace in temple ritual during illness while following medical treatment and resisting a promise of miracle cure.

passage:
"Vaibhav, you asked me on this podcast how I cope. I'm Jeevan, and the honest answer took me three years to find.

When the arthritis first took my knees, I was twenty-three and furious. I'd been a trekker. I kept trying to do everything like before and ended every week in bed.

Slowly, I learned to count energy like money. Five coins a day. A shower is one. Office is two. Cooking, one. That leaves one for something I love. Some days I spend it on a slow walk by the lake. Some days on bad comedy films with my nephew.

I ask for help now. My colleague carries my laptop bag, and I buy her chai.

People think acceptance means giving up. It's the opposite. I stopped fighting the body and started choosing. My new goal isn't the Himalayas. It's the lake, every Sunday, with a flask.

And I still make terrible jokes about my knees. They deserve it."

qa.q: How many coins of energy does Jeevan count each day?
qa.a: Five coins.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel about the illness now, compared with at first?
qa.a: At first Jeevan felt furious, but now feels calmer and accepting, even joking about the knees.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's habits shows acceptance without surrender?
qa.a: Counting energy in coins and choosing where to spend them, asking for help, and setting a new goal of walking by the lake.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's colleague see carrying the laptop bag?
qa.a: The colleague likely sees it as a small, easy kindness, and enjoys the chai in return.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone learning to live with the limits of illness, choosing how to spend energy, asking for help, redefining goals and keeping humour.

passage:
First week. After the diagnosis, Leela tried to keep her whole life exactly the same: full-time job, evening dance class, weekend trips. By Friday she was so drained she cried in the office bathroom. Her friend Sarika found her there.

Third week. Leela sat down with a notebook. What really mattered? Her work, some of it. Her mother. Dance, but maybe watching rather than performing. She told her manager she needed to work from home two days a week. It felt like losing, until the manager said yes without fuss.

Sixth week. On a Sunday afternoon Leela sat in the front row of the dance school, clapping for her students' first recital. She'd switched to teaching the little ones instead of performing. When a six-year-old tripped and bowed anyway, Leela laughed until her side hurt.

"You look happy," Sarika said, surprised.

"I am. Different life. Still mine."

qa.q: How many days a week did Leela ask to work from home?
qa.a: Two days a week.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she asked her manager to work from home?
qa.a: She felt a sense of loss and sadness, as though she were giving up, until the manager agreed easily.

qa.q: What did Leela do that helped her live with her limits?
qa.a: She listed what mattered most, asked for flexible work, and changed from performing to teaching dance, redefining her goals.

qa.q: How does Sarika see the change in Leela by the sixth week?
qa.a: Sarika is surprised and glad to see Leela happy again, after finding her crying in the bathroom weeks before.

grounding: Over several weeks, the passage shows a young woman learning to live with an illness's limits, redefining goals, asking for help and keeping joy and humour.

passage:
At 11 p.m., the power went out across Bhupen's building in Guwahati. The quarterly report was due to the client at nine the next morning, and his laptop battery showed twelve percent.

He sat in the dark and felt something ugly rise in his chest. Third late night this week. Fourth month of it. Nobody had said thank you since March. He'd started dreading Sundays so badly he couldn't eat dinner.

He texted his manager, Maria: "Power cut. I'll finish what I can. Honestly, I need to talk about my workload tomorrow."

He expected silence. She replied in five minutes. "Send what you have. Let's talk at ten."

At ten, he laid it out: the hours, the dread, how bitter he'd become. Maria listened. She moved one account to a colleague and told him to take next Friday off.

It wasn't everything. But he slept that night.

qa.q: What percentage of battery did Bhupen's laptop show?
qa.a: Twelve percent.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as he sat in the dark?
qa.a: He felt bitter and resentful after months of late nights with no thanks, along with dread about Sundays.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do instead of suffering in silence, and why did it help?
qa.a: He told his manager honestly about his workload and asked to talk, which led to lighter work and a day off.

qa.q: How might Maria see Bhupen's message?
qa.a: Maria may have been surprised by how overloaded he was, and responded quickly to fix it.

grounding: Under the pressure of a power cut and a deadline, the passage shows someone whose endless thanks-free overwork has bred bitterness and dread, and who talks to his manager about his load.

passage:
Sudha used to love her job at the Mumbai ad agency. Now she rolled her eyes at every new brief and muttered "same nonsense" under her breath. On Sunday evenings her stomach knotted, and she snapped at her flatmate for no reason.

On Monday morning, her team lead Ayesha piled on a new pitch due Wednesday. "You're our best," Ayesha said, already walking away.

Sudha wanted to shout. Instead she followed her to the pantry. "Can we talk for five minutes? I've worked three weekends in a row. I'm exhausted and honestly, I'm becoming bitter. I don't like who I am at work right now."

Ayesha stopped stirring her coffee. "I didn't realise it was that bad."

"I'd like to take the leave I have, the week after this pitch. And I need someone else on the retail account."

Ayesha nodded slowly. "Okay. Let's look at it together after lunch."

qa.q: How many weekends in a row had Sudha worked?
qa.a: Three weekends in a row.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Ayesha added the new pitch?
qa.a: She felt resentful and exhausted, wanting to shout after weeks of overwork.

qa.q: What did Sudha do that was mature, and why?
qa.a: She spoke to Ayesha about her load, asked for leave and help with the retail account, rather than silently suffering.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Sudha's workload after the talk?
qa.a: Ayesha is surprised, not having realised how bad it was, and agrees to look at it together.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose endless deadlines have bred cynicism and Sunday dread, who talks to her manager about load and asks for leave.

passage:
Sunaina had a fever, and the thesis was due in four days. She sat at her desk in the Kolkata hostel with a blanket round her shoulders, typing while her head throbbed. When her body begged her to lie down, a voice inside said: lazy.

At midnight, Disha, her roommate, came back from the library and stopped. "You're shivering."

"I can't stop. If I rest, I'm wasting time."

Disha felt her forehead. "Sunaina. You've slept four hours a night for two weeks. This isn't laziness. You're running on empty."

Sunaina started crying, which surprised them both.

Disha made her drink water and eat a banana. She turned off the laptop. "Sleep now. Tomorrow we'll email your guide and ask for two extra days. And if you still feel like this next week, go to the counsellor at the health centre."

Sunaina slept eleven hours. Her guide gave her three days.

qa.q: How many hours a night had Sunaina been sleeping?
qa.a: Four hours a night for two weeks.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel when she thought about resting?
qa.a: She felt guilty, as if resting meant being lazy and wasting time.

qa.q: What steps did Disha suggest, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Water, food, sleep, asking the guide for extra days, and seeing the counsellor if it continued, because burnout needs rest and help, not more pushing.

qa.q: How does Disha see Sunaina's exhaustion?
qa.a: Disha sees it as overload, not laziness, and is worried enough to step in firmly.

grounding: Under the pressure of a thesis deadline and fever, the passage shows someone who feels resting is lazy and keeps working while her body pleads, and a friend who helps her rest and seek help.

passage:
Trisha had not taken a day off since joining the Pune startup eight months ago. She answered emails in bed, ate lunch at her keyboard, and skipped her cousin's birthday. When she felt her heart race at night, she told herself it was coffee.

On Saturday, her friend Zeenat dragged her to the park. Trisha checked her phone every four minutes.

"When did you last sleep properly?" Zeenat asked.

"Resting makes me feel guilty. Everyone else is working."

"Everyone else also looks exhausted," Zeenat said. "That's not a good sign, Trisha."

They walked in silence. Then Trisha admitted she'd forgotten her own mother's call twice that week.

That evening she made a small plan: no email after nine, a walk every morning, dinner with a friend once a week. On Monday, she booked an appointment with a counsellor through the company's health plan. It felt strange. It also felt like the first sensible thing she'd done in months.

qa.q: How long had Trisha worked without a day off?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel when she thought about resting?
qa.a: She felt guilty, believing that resting while others worked was wrong.

qa.q: What small steps did Trisha choose, and why do they help?
qa.a: No email after nine, morning walks, weekly dinner with a friend and seeing a counsellor, because they treat burnout as overload that needs rest and support.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see Trisha's constant work?
qa.a: Zeenat sees it as a warning sign of exhaustion, not dedication, and worries about her friend.

grounding: The passage shows someone who feels resting is lazy and keeps working despite body signals, and who begins to sleep, move, see friends and get professional help.

passage:
Day one. Madhuri, Seema's manager, stopped at her desk. "You're so dependable. Can you take the Delhi client too? Nobody else could handle it." Seema said yes and felt proud.

Day twelve. Seema now had four accounts; her colleagues had two each. Her back hurt, she was eating dinner at ten, and Madhuri had just added a fifth. "You never let me down," Madhuri said. Seema smiled and felt something sink.

Day twenty. Seema spent a weekend morning writing it down: every account, hours worked, deadlines missed by others that she'd covered. She brought it to Madhuri with a list. "These are my priorities. I can do three accounts properly. Which two should move?"

Madhuri looked surprised, then flipped through the pages. "I didn't realise. Let's move the Delhi one and the new one."

Seema walked back to her desk, legs shaky. Saying no had been terrifying. It had also worked.

qa.q: How many accounts did Seema's colleagues have by day twelve?
qa.a: Two each.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling on day twelve when Madhuri added a fifth account?
qa.a: She felt a sinking dread and exhaustion behind her smile, since her reliability was only bringing more work.

qa.q: What did Seema do on day twenty, and why did it work?
qa.a: She documented her workload and proposed priorities, asking which accounts should move, which made the overload clear and let her say no.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Seema's workload at first?
qa.a: Madhuri sees Seema as dependable and doesn't notice the pile-up until she sees the written list.

grounding: Over several weeks, the passage shows a boss who praises dedication and piles on more, and a young woman who documents her workload, proposes priorities and says no.

passage:
"Reena, you keep saying yes to your boss. Let me tell you about my first job.

I, Sonali, was twenty-four, at a bank in Bhubaneswar. My manager called me 'our rock.' Every time I finished something, he gave me two more. 'You're so reliable,' he'd say, and I felt so proud. I was there till nine every night. I got headaches every day.

Then one evening I fainted on the bus home. The conductor had to call my father.

That frightened me into doing what I should have done earlier. I wrote down everything on my desk and the hours I worked, and I took it to my manager. I said, 'I can do these three well. Which ones go to someone else?'

He was angry for a day. Then he moved the work.

Don't wait for the bus, beta. Being reliable doesn't mean saying yes to everything."

qa.q: What did the manager call Sonali?
qa.a: "Our rock."

qa.q: What did Sonali feel when the manager praised that reliability?
qa.a: Sonali felt proud at first, even as the extra work brought daily headaches.

qa.q: What turning point in Sonali's story led to action, and what was done?
qa.a: Fainting on the bus frightened Sonali into documenting the workload and asking the manager which tasks to move.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Sonali's list?
qa.a: He was angry for a day, perhaps because he had relied on Sonali taking everything, but then accepted it and moved the work.

grounding: An elder recalls a boss who praised their reliability while piling on more, and how they documented the workload and proposed priorities after their health suffered.

passage:
Couples counsellor's note, session 2

Harish came alone today. His partner, Saurabh, was at work, as usual.

Harish described the last three months: Saurabh home at eleven, eating in silence, snapping when asked a simple question, falling asleep on the sofa with the laptop open. "I feel like I live with a stranger," Harish said. "Maybe he doesn't want me anymore."

I asked what Saurabh's work was like. Harish said a new project, a demanding boss, weekend calls. I suggested the withdrawal might be exhaustion, not rejection.

We practised what Harish might say, gently, without blame: "I miss you. I'm worried about you. Can we have Sunday breakfast together, phones off?"

Harish also said he'd been covering for Saurabh, cancelling plans with friends, making excuses to family. We talked about not silently enabling the overwork.

Next step: Harish will try the breakfast this Sunday and ask if Saurabh would join a session.

qa.q: What time did Saurabh come home over the last three months?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he said he lived with a stranger?
qa.a: He felt lonely and hurt, worried that Saurabh no longer wanted him.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Harish plan, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: A gentle message that he misses Saurabh, a phones-off Sunday breakfast, and not covering for the overwork, which invites connection without blame.

qa.q: How might Saurabh be feeling, based on what Harish describes?
qa.a: Saurabh seems exhausted and overloaded by the new project and boss, and his snapping may be tiredness rather than rejection.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows someone whose partner has become withdrawn and irritable from overwork, learning to say he misses him, propose small rituals, and not take the exhaustion as rejection or enable it.

passage:
Payal's diary. Wednesday.

Swati came home at midnight again. I'd kept dinner warm. She said "thanks" without looking up and went straight to her laptop. When I asked about her day, she said, "Please, not now," in a voice I didn't recognise.

I cried in the bathroom, quietly. For a while I've been wondering if she's tired of me.

But tonight I watched her fall asleep sitting up, glasses still on. She's not tired of me. She's tired.

So tomorrow I'm going to say it, gently: I miss you. I'm worried about how hard you're working. I'm not angry.

And I'm going to suggest one small thing. Chai together on the balcony before she opens the laptop, ten minutes, every morning. And I'll stop making excuses for her to her mother on Sundays. If she's too tired to call, she needs to see that.

I took her glasses off and put a blanket on her.

qa.q: What time did Swati come home?
qa.a: At midnight.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling while crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: Payal felt hurt and lonely, afraid that Swati had grown tired of Payal.

qa.q: What does Payal plan to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Say gently that Payal misses Swati, suggest ten minutes of chai each morning, and stop covering for the overwork, which reconnects without blame or enabling.

qa.q: How might Swati feel if she heard Payal's plan?
qa.a: Swati may feel relieved to hear Payal isn't angry, and perhaps guilty about how far work has taken her away.

grounding: The diary shows someone whose partner has become withdrawn from overwork, realising it is exhaustion not rejection, and planning to say they miss her, propose a small ritual and stop enabling it.

passage:
Ganga had a product launch in six days, and her team was two people short. She'd been leaving the flat in Hyderabad at seven and coming home at eleven for a month.

Tonight, walking in, she found Rekha asleep on the sofa. A plate covered with another plate sat on the table. Next to it, Rekha's phone showed a message Rekha had typed to a friend and never sent: "I feel like I'm married to a ghost."

Ganga stood there a long time. She'd been so focused on the launch she hadn't noticed.

She sat on the floor by the sofa. When Rekha woke, Ganga said, "I saw the message. I'm sorry. You're right."

"The launch..." Rekha began.

"Six days. I can't skip them. But from Monday, laptop off at eight, every night. And after the launch, the whole Sunday is ours. The lake, the old café."

Rekha squeezed her hand. "Just come home with your head too."

"I'll try. Tell me if I don't."

qa.q: How many days were left before the product launch?
qa.a: Six days.

passage:
It was Sarita's birthday, and Usha remembered at 9:40 p.m., still at her desk in the Andheri office.

She got home at eleven with a supermarket cake. Sarita was on the balcony, not crying, just quiet. "It's fine," she said, in the flat voice that meant it wasn't.

Usha sat down beside her. For months she'd been proud of her promotion, her late nights, the praise. She'd been telling herself it was all for their future. Looking at Sarita's face, she saw the future had been sitting alone on this balcony most evenings.

"It's not fine," Usha said. "I've been gone. Even when I'm here, I'm on my phone."

Sarita looked at her. "I miss you."

"I know. I'm setting a rule. Office laptop shuts at seven. Phone goes in the drawer at dinner. And this Saturday, you choose. Anything."

"The old bookshop and street food," Sarita said. "Like when we first met."

"Done," Usha said, and put her phone in her pocket, face down.

qa.q: What time did Usha remember Sarita's birthday?
qa.a: At 9:40 p.m.

qa.q: What did Usha feel looking at Sarita on the balcony?
qa.a: Usha felt guilty and sad, realising her ambition had left Sarita alone most evenings.

qa.q: What did Usha change, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: She set a seven o'clock laptop shut-off, no phone at dinner, and a shared Saturday of Sarita's choosing, to be present before resentment grows.

qa.q: How does Sarita experience Usha's long hours?
qa.a: Sarita feels lonely and missed, saying "It's fine" in a flat voice while clearly hurt.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose work has swallowed her evenings and left her partner alone, and who sets a shut-off time, plans a shared day and chooses to be present.
